## Section III: Comprehension 10 marks

**Read the passage below carefully and answer the questions that follow it. Use Correct English sentences, and as much as possible, your own words.**

Home Office figures show that in Britain in 1979, nearly 12,000 researchers subjected more than 4.7 million animals to experiments" presenting a risk of pain, distress, discomfort or interference to ordinary health or well-being". After most experiments, the animals were destroyed.

With the massive toll since 1948, the number of experiments has more than trebled. Animal Welfare Societies no longer present the only voice of protest. Scientists themselves are questioning whether the infliction of suffering on such a large scale call be justified.

Few would disagree. There was an outcry six years ago when it was revealed that in experiments on "new smoking materials" 48 beagles had been forced to inhale smoke for months before being killed and examined for lung damage.

Some scientists maintain that the anguish of animals is a regrettable but necessary price to pay for knowledge which has brought enormous benefits to mankind. For example, the discovery insulin estimated to have saved the lives of more than 50 million diabetics- stemmed from animal experiments, so did immunization against polio, typhoid, cholera and, diphtheria, and the development of artificial joints.

However, while Home Office struggles that more than four in five experiments on animals are for medical purposes, they give no indication how many of them involve quasi-medical products, developed purely for commercial profit What is clear is that a quarter of a million animals are used for non- medical testing of new products ranging from motor oils and polish, on the grounds that it is necessary to know the effects in case of accidental ingestion by humans.

More and more scientists are beginning to speak against the proliferation of animal test.

Animal experiment is often unnecessary both on humane and scientific grounds. Penicillin, for instance, is highly poisonous to guinea pigs, while thalidomide on pregnant animals gave no indications of the deformities it had caused in children.

Animal welfare Societies have swung from their crusade for the abolition of all animal experiments. They favour the approach of helping scientists find alternatives to animal techniques which can be not only more accurate but also cheaper. Already, a number of alternatives exist, The malignancy of tumors can be assessed by planting small pieces in hen's eggs, computers can be used in the design of new drugs, some cosmetic firms now can on human volunteers whereas 20 years ago, polio vaccine was produced in monkey kidney cell cultures requiring 200.000 monkeys a year, today it is made from test-tube cultures of human cells.

But alternatives are not used in every case, countless thousands of animals continue to die unnecessarily. A charter for laboratory animals is long overdue, and there is reason to believe that it will be strengthened by the now troubled consciences of many research scientists- well aware that both animals and mankind have similar capacities for suffering and that some knowledge can be obtained at too high a price.

**Questions**

1. What are the Home Office's findings on animal experiments? (1 mark)
2. Why do they use animals non-medical testing? (1 mark)
3. Give two benefits of animal experiments to man. (1 mark)
4. What besides animals can be used for testing? (1 mark)
5. a) Where do recent polio vaccines come from? (0.5 mark)
   b) How were they got in 1979? (0.5 mark)
6. Write a quarter of a million in figures. (1 mark)
7. What do the underlined words in the text refer to? (1 mark)
   they …………………………………………………………………………………………
   it …………………………………………………………………………………………

**Are these statements True or False?**

8. a) All animal experiments are for medical purposes (0.4mark) True ☐ False ☐
   b) Only Animal Welfare Societies are against animal experiments (0,5 mark) True ☐ False ☐
9. a) Scientists are troubled because the price of animal experiment is not high (0.5 mark) True ☐ False ☐
   b) Lack of accuracy is the scientific reason against animal experiment 1 (0.5 mark) True ☐ False ☐
10. Tick the right answer: (1 mark)
    a) The number of animal experiments trebled in : 1-. 10 years ☐ ; 2-. 31 years ☐ ; 3-. 20 years ☐
    b) Scientists find animal experiments
       1. acceptable on humane and scientific basis ☐
       2. unacceptable on humane and scientific basis ☐
       3. acceptable on humane but unacceptable on scientific basis ☐

### Rappel de méthode
Dans un exercice de "reading comprehension", chaque réponse doit être rédigée en anglais, en phrase complète, et reformulée avec ses propres mots autant que possible (la consigne l'exige explicitement ici : *"Use Correct English sentences, and as much as possible, your own words"*). La technique est toujours la même : repérer d'abord dans le texte la phrase exacte qui contient l'information, puis la reformuler en évitant de recopier le texte mot pour mot. Pour les questions Vrai/Faux, la justification doit toujours renvoyer à une phrase précise du texte.

**1. What are the Home Office's findings on animal experiments? (1 mark)**
*Réponse attendue :* "The Home Office found that in 1979, nearly 12,000 researchers in Britain used more than 4.7 million animals in experiments likely to cause them pain, distress or discomfort, and that most of these animals were later destroyed."

**2. Why do they use animals for non-medical testing? (1 mark)**
*Réponse attendue :* "Animals are used for non-medical testing because it is necessary to find out what effects new products, such as motor oils and polish, would have on humans in case they were accidentally swallowed."

**3. Give two benefits of animal experiments to man. (1 mark)**
*Réponse attendue :* "Animal experiments led to the discovery of insulin, which has saved the lives of more than 50 million diabetics, and to the development of vaccines against diseases such as polio, typhoid, cholera and diphtheria." (toute autre paire parmi les bénéfices cités - insuline, vaccins, articulations artificielles - est acceptée)

**4. What besides animals can be used for testing? (1 mark)**
*Réponse attendue :* "Besides animals, hen's eggs, computers, human volunteers and test-tube cultures of human cells can be used for testing."

**5. a) Where do recent polio vaccines come from? (0.5 mark)**
*Réponse attendue :* "Recent polio vaccines are made from test-tube cultures of human cells."
**b) How were they got in 1979? (0.5 mark)**
*Réponse attendue :* "In 1979, polio vaccines were produced in monkey kidney cell cultures, which required 200,000 monkeys a year."

### Piège à éviter
Pour la question 5.b, il ne faut pas répondre avec la méthode actuelle (cultures de cellules humaines) : le texte oppose explicitement "20 years ago" (l'ancienne méthode, sur cellules de rein de singe) et "today" (la méthode actuelle) - relire attentivement quel repère temporel correspond à la date demandée par la question évite l'erreur.

**6. Write a quarter of a million in figures. (1 mark)**
*Réponse attendue :* **250,000**

**7. What do the underlined words in the text refer to? (1 mark)**
*they* : renvoie à "Home Office" (l'organisme qui publie les chiffres et ne précise pas la part des produits quasi-médicaux dans les expériences à visée médicale).
*it* : renvoie à "thalidomide" (dans la phrase "thalidomide on pregnant animals gave no indications of the deformities **it** had caused in children").

### Piège à éviter
Le passage contient un autre "it" purement grammatical, sans antécédent réel ("it is necessary to know the effects…", "it will be strengthened…") : ce type de "it" impersonnel ne doit jamais être confondu avec un "it" de reprise, qui renvoie toujours à un nom précis mentionné juste avant.

**Vrai ou Faux ?**

**8. a)** All animal experiments are for medical purposes. **FAUX** - le texte précise que seuls "more than four in five" (plus de quatre expériences sur cinq) sont à visée médicale, pas la totalité.
**8. b)** Only Animal Welfare Societies are against animal experiments. **FAUX** - le texte indique que "scientists themselves are questioning" la pratique : les scientifiques eux-mêmes s'y opposent aussi, pas seulement les associations de protection animale.
**9. a)** Scientists are troubled because the price of animal experiment is not high. **FAUX** - c'est l'inverse : ils sont troublés parce que certaines connaissances sont obtenues "at too high a price" (à un prix trop élevé), pas parce qu'il est bas.
**9. b)** Lack of accuracy is the scientific reason against animal experiment. **VRAI** - le texte donne cette raison scientifique explicitement : les résultats obtenus sur l'animal sont parfois trompeurs (la pénicilline est toxique pour le cobaye, la thalidomide n'a montré aucun effet nocif chez l'animal alors qu'elle a causé des malformations chez l'enfant), et les alternatives proposées sont dites "more accurate" que les techniques sur l'animal.

### Conseil
Pour une question Vrai/Faux, cherche systématiquement dans le texte le mot qui contredit ou confirme l'affirmation (ici "more than four in five", "themselves", "too high a price", "more accurate") : le barème valorise la justification autant que la réponse elle-même, même si la consigne ne demande explicitement qu'une coche.

**10. a)** The number of animal experiments trebled in **31 years** *(1979 - 1948 = 31 ans, le texte précisant "with the massive toll since 1948, the number of experiments has more than trebled" en écho aux chiffres du Home Office datés de 1979)*.
**10. b)** Scientists find animal experiments **unacceptable on humane and scientific basis** *(le texte conclut explicitement : "Animal experiment is often unnecessary both on humane and scientific grounds")*.
